summary: This document describes the Schnorr non-interactive zero-knowledge proof, a variant of the three-pass Schnorr identification scheme. It lets someone prove they know a discrete logarithm without revealing it, and it can serve as a building block for other cryptographic protocols.

eli5.summary: It is a way to prove you know a secret without ever telling the secret. Like showing you can open a lock without handing over the key.

questions: what is a schnorr zero-knowledge proof
how to prove knowledge of a secret without revealing it
difference between interactive and non-interactive proofs
subtitle: Prove you know a secret without revealing it.

tldr.problem: In cryptographic protocols, it is often important to verify that the other party knows a secret without that party actually revealing the secret. For example, a participant might need to prove they know a private key without exposing it. Naive approaches leak information or require interaction, both of which are problematic in many settings.
tldr.mechanism: The Schnorr NIZK proof is a non-interactive variant of the classic Schnorr identification scheme. It uses a mathematical technique (the Fiat-Shamir transformation) to convert an interactive three-message protocol into a single proof that can be computed and verified without further exchange. The proof works by computing a challenge via a cryptographic hash function instead of receiving it from an external verifier, making it suitable for one-shot verification.
tldr.outcome: Participants in cryptographic protocols can prove knowledge of discrete logarithms (or equivalently, that they possess a specific private key) with high confidence while leaking no information beyond the fact that they know the secret. The technique works over both finite fields (like those used in DSA) and elliptic curves (like those used in ECDSA).

facts.label: Proof size (finite field)
facts.value: One element of Zp and one of Zq, typically 2048-3072 bits and 224-256 bits

facts.label: Soundness
facts.value: Adversary without secret has failure probability 2^(-t), where t is challenge bit length

facts.label: Required hash function
facts.value: Secure cryptographic hash (e.g., SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512)

today: RFC 8235 is Informational and describes the Schnorr NIZK proof without imposing new standards. The technique is well-established in cryptographic research and remains widely used in modern protocols, including recent work on password-authenticated key exchange and privacy-preserving authentication.

sections.title: Proving Knowledge Without Revealing
sections.content:
A fundamental principle in cryptography is: do not assume that a message you receive has a particular form unless you can verify it. For example, if you receive a value claimed to be g^r (meaning, 'g raised to the power r' for some secret r), you should not trust it is actually that form just because someone told you so.

The Schnorr non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proof is a technique to solve this problem. It allows one party (the prover) to prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a discrete logarithm without revealing any information about its value. A discrete logarithm is a secret exponent: if you know the secret value 'a', you can compute g^a (easy), but knowing g^a does not easily reveal 'a' (hard, assuming the discrete logarithm problem is intractable).

The name 'non-interactive' means the proof is a standalone object that can be checked without back-and-forth communication. The name 'zero-knowledge' means the proof leaks no information other than the fact that the prover knows the secret. These properties make the technique useful as a building block in many cryptographic protocols, from key exchange to certificate registration.
sections.eli5: You want to prove you know a secret number without telling anyone what it is. Zero-knowledge proof is like showing you can open a safe without revealing the combination.

sections.title: The Interactive Schnorr Identification Scheme
sections.content:
The Schnorr NIZK proof is derived from an older, interactive protocol called the Schnorr identification scheme. In that interactive version, Alice (the prover) and Bob (the verifier) exchange three messages.

First, Alice picks a random number v and sends Bob the value V = g^v. This is a commitment: Alice has locked in a random value without revealing what v is. Second, Bob picks a random challenge c and sends it to Alice. Third, Alice computes r = v - a*c (where a is her secret) and sends r to Bob. Bob then verifies the proof by checking that g^r * A^c equals V (where A = g^a is the public key). If the check passes, Bob is convinced that Alice knows the secret 'a'.

Why does this work? If Alice did not know 'a', she would have had to guess Bob's challenge c before committing to V. When Bob picks c after seeing V, Alice cannot retroactively make the math work unless she knows 'a'. Moreover, from Bob's perspective, the messages Alice sends (V and r) carry no information about 'a' itself because Alice chose v randomly.
sections.eli5: Alice picks a random number and locks it in a message (commitment). Bob challenges her. Alice responds in a way that only someone who knows the secret can do. The math works out if and only if she knows it.

sections.title: Making It Non-Interactive with Fiat-Shamir
sections.content:
The interactive protocol requires two round trips. To make it non-interactive, the RFC uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation: instead of having Bob provide a random challenge c, the prover computes c themselves by hashing their commitment together with other data. Specifically, c = H(g || V || A || UserID || OtherInfo), where H is a secure cryptographic hash function (such as SHA-256), || denotes concatenation, and OtherInfo is optional contextual data.

Because the hash function is deterministic and publicly known, the prover can compute c without waiting for input from the verifier. The proof then consists of just V and r (plus the user ID and any other info). The verifier computes the same hash to reconstruct c and checks that g^r * A^c equals V.

The security argument relies on modeling the hash function as a 'random oracle': it behaves as if an honest third party (the oracle) assigned a random value to each input. Under this model, the prover cannot predetermine what challenge they will get; they must commit to V first and accept whatever hash value results. This preserves the zero-knowledge property even though there is no actual verifier in the loop during proof generation.
sections.eli5: Instead of Bob picking the random challenge, Alice uses a hash function to pick it. Since the hash is public and deterministic, Bob can verify that she used it honestly. Now the proof is just two numbers, and anyone can check it without talking to Alice.

sections.title: Finite Fields and Elliptic Curves
sections.content:
The Schnorr NIZK proof can be implemented in two settings: over a finite field (similar to DSA) or over an elliptic curve (similar to ECDSA). The conceptual protocol is identical; only the underlying group operation changes.

In the finite field setting, group operations are modular exponentiation: g^a mod p. The parameters are primes p and q (where q divides p-1), and the group is the subgroup of order q. In the elliptic curve setting, group operations are point addition on the curve: G x [a] (scalar multiplication). The parameters are the curve equation and a base point G of prime order n.

The efficiency characteristics differ. Over a finite field, generating a proof requires roughly one modular exponentiation (computing g^v mod p), and verifying requires about two exponentiations (checking A^q mod p to validate the public key, and computing g^r * A^c mod p to verify the proof). Over an elliptic curve, generating a proof requires one scalar multiplication, and verifying requires one multiplication and a quick cofactor check. Elliptic curves are generally more efficient.
sections.eli5: The same idea works with two different kinds of math: regular modular arithmetic (like in DSA) or elliptic curve math (like in ECDSA). Both are secure; elliptic curves are just faster.

sections.title: Variants and Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The RFC describes a space-optimization variant where the prover sends (c, r) instead of (V, r). The verifier computes V = g^r * A^c and checks whether H(g || V || A || UserID || OtherInfo) equals the sent c. This saves space because V can be 2048 to 3072 bits while r is only 224 to 256 bits, and c is also 224 to 256 bits. However, the computation cost remains the same.

Real applications using Schnorr NIZK proofs include J-PAKE and YAK, two password-authenticated key exchange protocols. The RFC also mentions using the proof for proving possession of a private key during certificate registration with a Certification Authority. By including a CA name, expiry date, and other context in OtherInfo, the proof is bound to a specific registration procedure and cannot be replayed or used for a different purpose.

The inclusion of OtherInfo makes the proof flexible and context-aware. Each application can define what contextual information to include, ensuring that a proof generated for one purpose (e.g., authentication to Server A) cannot be reused for a different purpose (e.g., authentication to Server B) or in a different protocol.
sections.eli5: You can optimize the proof to be smaller by sending the challenge and answer instead of the commitment and answer. Also, you can include extra information (like the server name) to make sure the proof only works for the right situation.

sections.title: Security Foundations and Pitfalls
sections.content:
The Schnorr protocol (and its Fiat-Shamir variant) achieves three key security properties. Completeness: a prover who actually knows the discrete logarithm can always pass verification. Soundness: an adversary who does not know the logarithm has only a negligible chance (about 2^(-t), where t is the challenge bit length) of producing a valid proof. Honest-verifier zero-knowledge: the proof reveals only whether the prover knows the logarithm; it leaks no other information.

The RFC emphasizes a critical security requirement: a secure random number generator is essential. If the same random value v is reused with different challenges (or OtherInfo), an adversary can compute the secret by subtracting the two responses. Even slightly predictable randomness (e.g., v' = v + w for known w) enables attacks. This is a common pitfall in cryptographic implementations.

Another consideration is replay attacks. An adversary might replay a proof to trick a verifier or introduce undesirable correlations in a protocol. The inclusion of a unique UserID in the hash prevents the prover from verifying their own proof. Applications must also consider whether other replay scenarios (e.g., using the same proof with different parties) are possible and include sufficient context in OtherInfo to prevent them.
sections.eli5: The proof is mathematically sound if you use good random numbers and you check that the proof is for the right person and right situation. Reusing random numbers or forgetting who the proof is for can break security.
